title: Bridging Radiology and Pathology via Concept-Based Co-Adaptation
one_liner: Use medical concepts doctors actually use as a shared language to make radiology and pathology AI models work together, using almost no extra weights.
lead: Hospitals often need a diagnosis that combines images from two different sources: a radiology scan (like an X-ray) and a pathology slide (tissue under a microscope). A doctor reads both. But most AI systems train only on one kind of image at a time. This paper shows how to take two separately trained AI models and make them speak the same language—through the medical concepts (like 'tumor grade' or 'cell density') that doctors use in both domains—without retraining them from scratch.

paras: A radiology model (trained on thousands of X-rays and scans) learns to see patterns in those images. A pathology model (trained on tissue slides) learns completely different patterns. When you want both for one diagnosis, you have a problem: they are like two people who speak different languages and have never met.

A beginner might try to just glue the two model predictions together with a simple average or a vote. This fails because the models say completely different things about the same disease. The radiology model might focus on size and shape; the pathology model might focus on cell type and density. They are measuring different things, so averaging their confidence scores is like averaging opinions from two people who do not share the same frame of reference.

callout.html: Use medical concepts that doctors apply in both domains—concepts like 'tumor grade' or 'necrosis'—as a shared semantic bridge. Both models produce concept scores, and you align those scores before fusing the final prediction.

steps.text: Radiology model: Does this scan show tumor grade 3? Pathology model: Does this tissue show grade 3? Both output confidence scores.
The scores from both models are adjusted so they agree on the scale. A prompting mechanism learns which parts of each image matter.
A small scoring network compares the two models' concept scores and learns to bring them closer together.
Now that both models speak the same language, combine their aligned concept scores into one final prediction.

steps.b: Train only the bridges, not the models
steps.text: The original radiology and pathology models stay frozen. Only the alignment layer and fusion layer are trained—just 0.15% extra weights.

paras: The paper freezes the two pretrained models and adds a thin new layer: a concept-alignment module. This module learns to translate one model's concept scores into the same scale as the other. It is a bridge, not a retraining.

hidden.name: how well each model's concept confidence matches the other
paras: When both models see the same patient, they output confidence scores for each medical concept—like 'grade 3' or 'cell density.' The alignment score measures how close those two numbers are. If the radiology model says 'grade 3: 0.8' and the pathology model says 'grade 3: 0.75,' the alignment is good. If one says 0.8 and the other says 0.2, they disagree, and the alignment score is low.

The paper uses a small trainable network to learn which concepts should be aligned and how much each concept matters for the final diagnosis. It gives a higher weight to concepts where both models agree, and it lets each model's unique strengths shine where they differ.

heat.caption: Darker concepts show stronger alignment between radiology and pathology models. Highlights show the top three concepts guiding the diagnosis.

reads.html: The alignment score tells you how much both AI models agree on the medical concepts present in a patient's images. High agreement means both models saw the same clue.

The paper learns a scoring function that maps each model's internal concept representation (the patterns the model learned for each concept) to a shared alignment space, bringing the radiology and pathology patterns closer together for the same concept.

mechanism.h2: Why aligning concepts fixes the fusion problem
paras: The root cause of poor fusion is that the two models were trained on different data, in isolation. A radiology model learns what size and shape matter for disease. A pathology model learns what cell types and density matter. They have no common ground. When you ask them both 'What is the confidence?' you get back two numbers that mean completely different things—like comparing temperature in Celsius to temperature in Fahrenheit without converting.

This paper fixes it by finding a shared semantic layer: medical concepts. Both models can output scores for the same concepts because doctors use the same vocabulary in both domains. The trick is learning HOW to extract those concept scores from each model and THEN aligning them so that when both models see the same concept, they say similar things. A small learnable prompting mechanism (called GCSP, Global-Context-Shared Prompt) learns to extract the right concept signals from each model by weighting the parts of each image that matter most (giving more importance to tissue that looks abnormal, less importance to background).

Once concept scores are aligned, fusion becomes straightforward: you just combine them because they now speak the same language. The paper learns which concepts are most reliable (via attention weights in the fusion step), so high-confidence, well-aligned concepts drive the final diagnosis.

stages.s: Each model extracts concept scores (is this grade 3? is this necrotic?)
Alignment layer learns to put both sets of scores on the same scale
Fusion network combines aligned concept scores weighted by confidence
One final diagnosis from both domains

math.words: penalty equals the distance between each model's concept score and the other model's concept score (after adjustment), plus the final loss if the fused prediction is wrong
math.equation: L_total = L_fusion(fuse(align_rad(C_rad), align_path(C_path)), y) + lambda * sum_j ||align_rad(C_rad_j) - align_path(C_path_j)||^2

the concept scores from the pathology model
small neural networks that adjust each model's concept scores to a shared scale
combines the aligned concept scores into a final prediction
the true diagnosis (0 or 1, healthy or diseased)
the loss function measuring how wrong the fused prediction is
how much to reward alignment (typically 0.1 to 1.0)
the squared distance between the two aligned concept scores

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Concept: Tumor Grade 3. Radiology model outputs 0.7, Pathology model outputs 0.5.
Alignment layer adjusts: align_rad(0.7) = 0.68, align_path(0.5) = 0.68. Now they agree.
Concept: Necrosis Present. Radiology outputs 0.2, Pathology outputs 0.8.
After alignment: align_rad(0.2) = 0.4, align_path(0.8) = 0.6. Still different.
Distance: ||0.4 - 0.6||^2 = 0.04. Penalty: 1.0 * 0.04 = 0.04. Training will nudge these closer.
Final prediction combines [0.68, 0.4, ...other aligned concepts...] to predict cancer: yes/no.

math.note: The equation pulls the two models' concept scores toward each other during training, so they say similar things about the same medical concepts.

charts.title: This paper (concept-aligned fusion)
charts.note: Both modalities, aligned concepts, only 0.15% extra trainable weights.

items.html: A concept like 'tumor grade' might be clear in pathology (defined by pathologists for decades) but fuzzy in radiology (radiologists judge grade indirectly from size and shape). If the radiology model never learned a strong internal representation for 'grade,' the alignment layer cannot extract it, and alignment fails. The paper uses only concepts validated in both domains.

If the radiology model is very confident and the pathology model is unsure, the fusion might just follow radiology, ignoring pathology. This happens if the alignment loss is too weak (lambda too small) or if the fusion network learns to ignore low-confidence concepts. The paper weights each concept by its alignment quality and confidence.

The alignment layer is small but trainable. If the training set is small, it might learn spurious alignments specific to that dataset, not real medical concepts. The paper mitigates this by freezing the main models (no overfitting there) and gently steering the alignment layer toward smooth, generalizable concepts (via weight decay and early stopping).

items.b: Done right: both modalities strengthen each other.
items.html: When both models agree strongly on a concept (high alignment, high confidence), that concept drives the diagnosis because both sources confirm it. When they disagree, the fusion network learns to weight each model's concept score by how confident and aligned that score is—giving more weight to high-confidence predictions because they have fewer chances of being wrong in the final decision. So the final diagnosis uses the strengths of each modality where each is most trustworthy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a minimal multimodal diagnosis system on two real (or synthetic) patients. Take a radiology image and a pathology image from the same patient. Load both pretrained models. Extract concept scores from each (e.g. 'tumor grade 0-4', 'necrosis yes/no'). Train the alignment and fusion layers on a small training set (10-50 patient pairs). Measure how well alignment improves the joint diagnosis compared to a naive average of the two models' class probabilities, because the average treats all concepts as equally important regardless of whether the two models actually agree on them or how confident each one is about its predictions.
demo.closing: The demo must show that concept-aligned fusion gives measurably better diagnosis than just averaging two separate model predictions, using nearly no extra trainable weights—because alignment ensures that both models' predictions are on the same scale before combining them, so when both say the same thing, you can trust it, and when they differ, you know which one is more confident.
